title: Missouri Voters Just Made It Much Harder for Lawmakers to Overturn Citizen-Led Initiatives
author: Jeremy Kohler
content:
Across the country on Tuesday, voters delivered a wave of Democratic
victories, flipping seats in Congress as well as state legislatures, and
weakening a number of Republican majorities.

Missouri was no exception. Democrats made significant gains in the state
House, picking up 16 seats, though Republicans still hold every statewide
office and maintain control of the legislature.

Nonetheless, the election was more than just a rebuke of President Donald
Trump. It reflected a long-simmering frustration with Missouri politicians
who, time and again, have sought to override the will of voters — a practice
that has intensified under years of Republican control. What’s more, voters
went beyond weakening the Republican majority. They approved a constitutional
amendment that curtailed the powers of the legislature and shifted more
authority directly to the people.

Amendment 6, approved by a decisive margin, sharply limits the legislature’s
ability to overturn laws and constitutional amendments enacted through citizen
initiatives, and its ability to revive laws voters rejected through
referendums.

Missouri Republicans have only themselves to blame, according to political
observers who have watched the conflict between lawmakers and voters
intensify. They resisted a voter-approved Medicaid expansion, repealed paid
sick leave protections and sought to reverse abortion rights. They sometimes
packaged their efforts with unrelated culture-war provisions, like limiting
healthcare for transgender minors, that were intended to appeal to
conservative voters.

Then they tried to persuade voters this summer to surrender some of their own
power by changing the constitution to make it harder to pass initiatives in
the first place. Voters rejected that proposal [by more than a 4-to-1
margin](https://www.stlpr.org/government-politics-issues/2026-08-04/missouri-
amendment-4-amend-state-constitution).

“I think the people of Missouri are trying to wrest control back from our
legislature because our legislature at this point does not seem to really be
representing the majority view in the state,” said Jayne Woods, a professor at
the University of Missouri law school who has written about the tension
between direct democracy and legislative power.

Benjamin Singer is the co-founder and executive director of the Respect
Missouri Voters campaign, which helped organize the push for Amendment 6. He
said the frustration stretched back decades, including periods when Democrats
controlled the legislature. He said when the campaign began organizing in late
2024, many volunteers were still angry about lawmakers’ decision in 2011 to
weaken [restrictions on puppy mills](https://www.stlmag.com/Puppy-Mill-Fiasco-
Shows-the-True-Colors-of-the-Missouri-Legislature/) that voters had approved
just a year earlier.

The campaign, he said, had already built a substantial volunteer operation
before Republican lawmakers moved in 2025 to undo voter-approved measures that
were intended to mandate paid sick leave and protect abortion rights. Respect
Missouri Voters ultimately gathered enough signatures to put Amendment 6 on
the ballot, seeking not only to protect the initiative process but to
strengthen the electorate’s power over the legislature.

With the passage of that amendment, lawmakers now must get 80% support in both
the House and Senate before they can propose changing or repealing measures
enacted through citizen initiatives, or move to revive laws voters rejected
through referendums. Even then, voters must approve any change in a statewide
election. The restriction applies to measures voters have approved since 2010,
including the constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights that voters
approved in 2024.

Republican lawmakers put a measure on Tuesday’s ballot to [restore abortion
restrictions](https://www.propublica.org/article/missouri-abortion-gender-
transition-minors-amendment-3), but voters [rejected that,
too](https://www.stltoday.com/news/local/government-
politics/article_b52ff175-171b-4bee-8a43-9792d4646d51.html#tracking-
source=home-top-story). With the passage of Amendment 6, abortion opponents
don’t have a clear path to try again.

![A room full of people cheer, clap and wave their hands in the
air.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2302992744_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Brian
Wingbermuehle and Mallory Schwarz, center, both with Abortion Action Missouri,
celebrate election results at a Stop the Ban watch party in St. Louis. David
Carson/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images

Amendment 6 also strengthens the referendum process. In addition to
restricting lawmakers’ ability to reenact laws similar to those voters have
rejected, the amendment explicitly protects the right of citizens to enact
laws and constitutional amendments with a simple statewide majority, rejecting
the higher threshold Republican lawmakers had sought to impose earlier this
year. And it safeguards the power of Missouri’s courts to rewrite misleading
ballot language, a power that Republican officials have repeatedly tried to
strip away.

The result, political observers said, could make the legislature less
consequential than it once was. Republicans still have the votes to pass most
laws, but when voters reject those laws at the ballot box or enact their own
measures or constitutional amendments through citizen initiatives, lawmakers
will now face significant obstacles to overriding them.

Denny Hoskins, the secretary of state and one of Amendment 6’s most prominent
Republican opponents, acknowledged how profoundly it would change the balance
of power. Before the election, he [told the Missouri
Independent](https://missouriindependent.com/2026/09/22/amendment-6-could-
make-another-missouri-congressional-gerrymander-much-harder/) that if the
amendment passed, “it will basically cut our legislature off at the knees as
far as being able to pass laws to reduce crime and cut taxes.”

In text messages on Wednesday, Hoskins said that Amendment 6 weakens the
legislature and governor “regardless of party” and predicted that it would be
challenged in court. He said that “giving power back to the people” might be a
great slogan but that the amendment’s sponsors “have no idea what this
actually will do.”

Hoskins himself had tried to keep Amendment 6 off the ballot. In August, he
refused to certify the initiative petition, arguing that it violated
constitutional restrictions on ballot measures. He also rejected a separate
petition seeking a statewide referendum on a newly gerrymandered congressional
map that Republican lawmakers, working at Trump’s behest, had approved to give
their party another seat in Congress.

The Missouri Supreme Court overruled him in both cases, ordering that the
measures appear on the ballot. The court found Hoskins in contempt when he
sought to use the map in spite of its ruling. Hoskins backed down and the
justices did not have him arrested.

![A man wearing a red suit speaks into numerous microphones that a crowd of
people hold toward him.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2294033023_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Missouri
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins speaks to members of the press after the
Missouri Supreme Court found him in contempt over the use of new Missouri
congressional maps. Hoskins backed down and the justices did not have him
arrested. Liz Rymarev, St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images

On Tuesday, voters rejected the map too. With Amendment 6 now in place — and
Democrats significantly bolstering their numbers in the House — Republican
lawmakers aren’t likely to gather enough support to override the voters’
rejection of their map.

Travis Crum, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis and an
expert on voting rights and election law, said he knew of no other state with
a restriction quite like Missouri’s 80% threshold. But he said the amendment
was understandable given the legislature’s repeated attempts to reverse voter-
approved policies and its unsuccessful effort this summer to make citizen
initiatives harder to pass.

“I think that there’s just been this boiling frustration with how the
legislature has ignored the initiative process and then sort of tried to
rewrite it to its own ends,” he said.

John Hancock, a former Missouri Republican Party chair and longtime GOP
consultant, acknowledged that Republican lawmakers had brought some of the
backlash on themselves. But he warned that Amendment 6 could make Missouri a
magnet for well-financed out-of-state interest groups seeking to enact laws
through ballot initiatives — possibly on taxation or gun policy.

That [concern about wealthy outside
interests](https://www.propublica.org/article/mike-kehoe-missouri-
amendment-5-dark-money) was also central to the Republican-backed proposal to
restrict citizen initiatives that voters rejected in August. Gov. Mike Kehoe
had spent months warning voters about out-of-state special interests trying to
rewrite the state constitution, even while a campaign supporting his proposal
to phase out the state income tax benefited from funding from a Delaware
nonprofit with undisclosed donors.

Woods said the defeat suggested voters weren’t persuaded by that argument.
Regardless of who finances an initiative campaign, she noted, Missourians are
the ones organizing, gathering support and ultimately deciding whether to
approve the measures.

“I think that the people of the state pretty resoundingly said, ‘No, we don’t
believe that that’s true,’” Woods said. “‘We believe this is our citizens who
are doing this. This is what we want as citizens.’”

The post [Missouri Voters Just Made It Much Harder for Lawmakers to Overturn
Citizen-Led Initiatives](https://www.propublica.org/article/missouri-voter-
ballot-initiatives-amendment-6) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
